newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed insists has Clinton invite.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed insists has Clinton invite.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed insisted on Thursday that he had a personal invitation from Bill Clinton to attend the U.S. president's inauguration despite an official denial from the United States.
"I am invited to the inauguration of the president of the United States of America," Lebed told Russia's NTV commercial television. "I am invited by the president."
Any change in that plan, he speculated, could be the result of scheming between Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

The tough-talking retired general, hired and fired as Yeltsin's security adviser in the space of four months last summer, was first quoted on Tuesday as saying he had accepted an invitation to next Monday's ceremony in Washington.

But the U.S. embassy in Moscow issued a statement on Thursday denying Clinton had invited the ex-paratrooper, who has predicted he will have succeeded the ailing Yeltsin by the end of the year and has upset the West with nationalist rhetoric.
"General Alexander Lebed has not been invited," the statement from embassy press spokesman Richard Hoagland said.
Only Russia's ambassador to Washington had been invited by the White House to represent the Russian government, it said.
It went on to say, however, that the embassy "understood" Lebed had been invited by members of Congress and hoped to attend the inauguration as a private citizen.
Asked by NTV, however, whether he had confused a congressional invitation with one from the White House, Lebed insisted he had checked again with Washington.
"I am invited by the president," he repeated.

Speculating on the reasons for the apparent contradictions, Lebed said: "It's possible some internal manoeuvring has started, linked mainly to the friendship between the presidents of the United States and Russia. I don't rule that out. All the same, I am invited to the inauguration and I will be there."

Lebed, 46, who came third in last July's presidential election, was speaking by telephone from Germany, where he is on a five-day visit to introduce himself as a potential Russian leader. Some politicians have criticised German Chancellor Helmut Kohl for failing to meet the Russian general.
